sentences.text: Temnodontosaurus is generally estimated to be 9 meters long, making it one of the largest known ichthyosaurs.
Although it is one of the largest ichthyosaurs known, it is not as large as Triassic forms like Shonisaurus or Ichthyotitan.
This animal represents the largest known ichthyosaur within the parvipelvian group.
Its eye sockets were wider than 25 cm, possibly giving it the largest eyes in the animal kingdom.
The creature had a snout longer than its lower jaw, which was equipped with sharp teeth.
Based on complete skeletons, Temnodontosaurus is estimated to have had more than 40 presacral vertebrae.
The first known fossil was a complete skull and partial skeleton found by Joseph and Mary Anning in the early 1810s in Dorset, England.
Joseph Anning discovered the first skull around 1810 on the cliffs of Black Ven in Dorset, England.
Sir Everard Home analyzed the first specimen between 1814 and 1819, making it the first ichthyosaur to be scientifically described.
William Conybeare assigned the first Temnodontosaurus specimen to the species Ichthyosaurus platyodon in 1822.
Richard Lydekker proposed the genus name Temnodontosaurus in 1889 due to large dental differences with other Ichthyosaurus species.
The type species of Temnodontosaurus is Ichthyosaurus platyodon.
Recognized species of Temnodontosaurus include T. trigonodon, T. crassimanus, T. zetlandicus, and T. nuertingensis.
Friedrich von Huene transferred the species to the genus Leptopterygius in 1931.
The family Temnodontosauridae was established in 1974 to include the genus Temnodontosaurus.
Temnodontosaurus lived during the Lower Hettangian to Toarcian stages.
Specimens of T. platyodon, T. trigonodon, and T. crassimanus have been estimated to reach a body length of around 9 meters.
Phylogenetic analyses suggest Temnodontosaurus is currently a polyphyletic taxon and requires revision.
The species T. eurycephalus and T. azerguensis are considered disputed within the genus Temnodontosaurus.
McGowan and Motani noted that further research could question the validity of T. crassimanus.
McGowan and Motani considered the species a nomen dubium in 2003, but its validity and genus assignment are maintained in subsequent studies.
McGowan distinguished T. risor from other species based on larger orbits, smaller maxillae, and a curved snout.
In 1995, McGowan revised his earlier work and found that the three specimens attributed to T. risor were actually juveniles of T. platyodon, with previous distinctions being growth stages.
